claim: Interplay between dopaminergic and cholinergic neuromodulation in the striatum is crucial for movement control.
source: Interplay between dopaminergic and cholinergic neuromodulation in the striatum is crucial for movement control, with prominent models proposing pro-kinetic and anti-kinetic effects of dopamine and acetylcholine release, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Prominent models propose pro-kinetic effects of dopamine release in the striatum.
source: Interplay between dopaminergic and cholinergic neuromodulation in the striatum is crucial for movement control, with prominent models proposing pro-kinetic and anti-kinetic effects of dopamine and acetylcholine release, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as an existing model in the field, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Prominent models propose anti-kinetic effects of acetylcholine release in the striatum.
source: Interplay between dopaminergic and cholinergic neuromodulation in the striatum is crucial for movement control, with prominent models proposing pro-kinetic and anti-kinetic effects of dopamine and acetylcholine release, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as an existing model in the field, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Bursts across the cholinergic population occurred at transitions between movement states.
source: Bursts across the cholinergic population occurred at transitions between movement states and were marked by widespread network synchronization which diminished during sustained locomotion.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1, 3, and 4.

claim: Cholinergic population bursts at movement state transitions were marked by widespread network synchronization.
source: Bursts across the cholinergic population occurred at transitions between movement states and were marked by widespread network synchronization which diminished during sustained locomotion.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Cholinergic network synchronization diminished during sustained locomotion.
source: Bursts across the cholinergic population occurred at transitions between movement states and were marked by widespread network synchronization which diminished during sustained locomotion.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Cholinergic and dopaminergic signals in dorsal striatum are distinct but coordinated on sub-second timescales.
source: Simultaneous cholinergic and dopaminergic recordings revealed distinct but coordinated sub-second signals, suggesting a new model where cholinergic population synchrony signals rapid changes in movement states while dopamine signals the drive to enact or sustain those states.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5-7.

claim: Cholinergic population synchrony signals rapid changes in movement states.
source: Simultaneous cholinergic and dopaminergic recordings revealed distinct but coordinated sub-second signals, suggesting a new model where cholinergic population synchrony signals rapid changes in movement states while dopamine signals the drive to enact or sustain those states.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental data shown in Figures 1-7.

claim: Dopamine signals the drive to enact or sustain movement states.
source: Simultaneous cholinergic and dopaminergic recordings revealed distinct but coordinated sub-second signals, suggesting a new model where cholinergic population synchrony signals rapid changes in movement states while dopamine signals the drive to enact or sustain those states.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental data shown in Figures 5-7.

claim: Striatum cholinergic interneurons are critical for normal functioning of the basal ganglia in the control of movement.
source: Striatum cholinergic interneurons (ChIs) have long been recognized as critical for normal functioning of the basal ganglia in the control of movement and in learning and responding to motivational and salient stimuli (Apicella et al., 1996; Apicella et al., 1997; Apicella et al., 1991; Collins et al., 2016; Kimura et al., 1984; Kondabolu et al., 2016; Schulz et al., 2011; Kaneko et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cholinergic interneurons comprise approximately 1-3% of the total cell population in striatum.
source: Although they comprise a small proportion of the total cell population (~1–3%) in striatum (Kimura et al., 1980), they are believed to contribute to debilitating motor and cognitive symptoms in a range of disorders including Parkinson's Disease (PD) (McGeer et al., 1961; Barbeau, 1962; Tanimura et al., 2018; Bordia et al., 2016a; Bordia et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation to Kimura et al., 1980.

claim: Cholinergic interneurons contribute to debilitating motor and cognitive symptoms in Parkinson's Disease.
source: Although they comprise a small proportion of the total cell population (~1–3%) in striatum (Kimura et al., 1980), they are believed to contribute to debilitating motor and cognitive symptoms in a range of disorders including Parkinson's Disease (PD) (McGeer et al., 1961; Barbeau, 1962; Tanimura et al., 2018; Bordia et al., 2016a; Bordia et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Anti-cholinergic (muscarinic) drugs are recognized as the earliest treatment capable of alleviating some of the debilitating movement deficits characteristic of Parkinson's Disease.
source: Anti-cholinergic (muscarinic) drugs are recognized as the earliest treatment capable of alleviating some of the debilitating movement deficits characteristic of PD (McGeer et al., 1961; Barbeau, 1962; Tanimura et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Loss of dopaminergic innervation to the dorsal striatum from the substantia nigra pars compacta in Parkinson's Disease disrupts a dynamic balance between acetylcholine and dopamine signaling.
source: This clinical observation led to the hypothesis that loss of dopaminergic (DA) innervation to the dorsal striatum from the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) in PD disrupts a dynamic balance between acetylcholine and dopamine signaling (Barbeau, 1962).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on clinical observations, supported by citation to Barbeau, 1962.

claim: Unilateral ablation of cholinergic interneurons results in ipsilateral turning behavior opposite to the effects of unilateral dopamine terminal lesions.
source: Unilateral ablation of ChIs results in ipsilateral turning behavior opposite to the effects of unilateral DA terminal lesions (Kaneko et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as an established finding supported by citation to Kaneko et al., 2000.

claim: Cholinergic signaling opposes the pro-kinetic actions of dopamine in the striatum.
source: These findings suggest that cholinergic signaling opposes the pro-kinetic actions of dopamine in the striatum.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from cited studies on optogenetic manipulations.

claim: Naturally occurring signaling patterns of dopamine input to the striatum during movement have been described.
source: However, while naturally occurring signaling patterns of DA input to the striatum during movement have been described (Howe and Dombeck, 2016; Patriarchi et al., 2018), signaling in cholinergic interneuron networks, and the precise coordination between ChI and DA signaling occurring during movements, remain unclear.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to Howe and Dombeck, 2016; Patriarchi et al., 2018.

claim: Signaling in cholinergic interneuron networks during movements remains unclear.
source: However, while naturally occurring signaling patterns of DA input to the striatum during movement have been described (Howe and Dombeck, 2016; Patriarchi et al., 2018), signaling in cholinergic interneuron networks, and the precise coordination between ChI and DA signaling occurring during movements, remain unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The precise coordination between cholinergic interneuron and dopamine signaling occurring during movements remains unclear.
source: However, while naturally occurring signaling patterns of DA input to the striatum during movement have been described (Howe and Dombeck, 2016; Patriarchi et al., 2018), signaling in cholinergic interneuron networks, and the precise coordination between ChI and DA signaling occurring during movements, remain unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Extracellular single-unit recordings of tonically active, putative cholinergic interneurons have revealed rapid (<200 ms latency), synchronized responses to salient, neutral and positive and negative conditioned stimuli.
source: In behaving rodents and primates, extracellular single-unit recordings of tonically active, putative ChIs (TANs) have revealed rapid (<200 ms latency), synchronized responses to salient, neutral and positive and negative conditioned stimuli and to primary rewards and punishments (Apicella et al., 1996; Apicella et al., 1991; Kimura et al., 1984; Aosaki et al., 1994a; Ravel et al., 1999; Ravel et al., 2003; Morris et al., 2004; Apicella, 2017; Blazquez et al., 2002), but rarely to spontaneous movements.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Tonically active neurons rarely respond to spontaneous movements.
source: In behaving rodents and primates, extracellular single-unit recordings of tonically active, putative ChIs (TANs) have revealed rapid (<200 ms latency), synchronized responses to salient, neutral and positive and negative conditioned stimuli and to primary rewards and punishments (Apicella et al., 1996; Apicella et al., 1991; Kimura et al., 1984; Aosaki et al., 1994a; Ravel et al., 1999; Ravel et al., 2003; Morris et al., 2004; Apicella, 2017; Blazquez et al., 2002), but rarely to spontaneous movements.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior electrophysiology studies.

claim: Stimulus evoked tonically active neuron responses often consist of an initial pause in firing rate followed by a burst in firing rate.
source: Stimulus evoked TAN responses often consist of an initial pause in firing rate (occasionally preceded by a short burst of firing) followed by a burst in firing rate.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior electrophysiology studies.

claim: The magnitude and duration of the pause/burst in tonically active neurons is modulated by learning.
source: The magnitude and duration of the pause/burst is modulated by learning and depend in some cases on the nigrostriatal dopamine system (Ravel et al., 2003; Aosaki et al., 1994b; Aosaki et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to Ravel et al., 2003; Aosaki et al., 1994b; Aosaki et al., 1995.

claim: The magnitude and duration of the pause/burst in tonically active neurons depend in some cases on the nigrostriatal dopamine system.
source: The magnitude and duration of the pause/burst is modulated by learning and depend in some cases on the nigrostriatal dopamine system (Ravel et al., 2003; Aosaki et al., 1994b; Aosaki et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to Ravel et al., 2003; Aosaki et al., 1994b; Aosaki et al., 1995.

claim: Striatum cholinergic interneuron signaling may play a role, along with dopamine, in modulating long term plasticity for goal directed learning.
source: These findings indicate that striatum ChI signaling may play a role, along with DA, in modulating long term plasticity for goal directed learning (Aosaki et al., 1994b).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from cited findings, supported by citation to Aosaki et al., 1994b.

claim: Tonically active neuron bursts and pauses to conditioned and salient sensory stimuli have been proposed to drive rapid attentional orienting, goal-directed action, and set-shifting.
source: Based on recordings and manipulations, TAN bursts and pauses to conditioned and salient sensory stimuli have also been proposed to drive rapid attentional orienting, goal-directed action, and set-shifting (Collins et al., 2016; Ding et al., 2010; Aoki et al., 2018; Aoki et al., 2015; Atallah et al., 2014; Tzavos et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as a proposed mechanism supported by citations to Collins et al., 2016; Ding et al., 2010; Aoki et al., 2018; Aoki et al., 2015; Atallah et al., 2014; Tzavos et al., 2004.

claim: Two studies in freely moving rodents have described heterogeneous positive and negative responses in dorsal and ventral striatum tonically active neurons aligned to movements during a reward-directed instrumental task.
source: Two studies in freely moving rodents have described heterogeneous positive and negative responses in dorsal and ventral striatum TANs aligned to movements during a reward-directed instrumental task (Yarom and Cohen, 2011; Benhamou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to Yarom and Cohen, 2011; Benhamou et al., 2014.

claim: In primates, tonically active neurons do not generally respond to simple cued arm movements.
source: In primates, TANs do not generally respond to simple cued arm movements, but one study described small responses to self-timed movements (Lee et al., 2006) and another showed a relationship between cue evoked TAN responses and the probability to respond in eye blink conditioning (Blazquez et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior primate studies.

claim: It remains unclear whether movement-related tonically active neuron responses reflect instrumental task contingencies, cue responses or changes in movement per se.
source: However, it remains unclear whether these movement-related TAN responses reflect instrumental task contingencies, cue responses or changes in movement per se.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: In-vivo extracellular unit studies have been limited in their ability to discriminate true cholinergic interneurons from other striatal cell types.
source: Moreover, in-vivo extracellular unit studies have been limited in their ability to discriminate true ChI responses from other striatal cell types (Atallah et al., 2014; Gage et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of prior studies, supported by citations to Atallah et al., 2014; Gage et al., 2010.

claim: It remains unclear how or whether cholinergic interneurons participate in spontaneous movement control independently of discrete action-outcome contingencies, outcome predicting cues, or salient external stimuli.
source: Thus, it remains unclear how or whether ChIs participate in spontaneous movement control independently of discrete action-outcome contingencies, outcome predicting cues, or salient external stimuli.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Cholinergic interneurons are capable of bi-directionally influencing cell-type specific excitability of both medium spiny projection neurons and striatal interneurons.
source: From these studies, a complex picture has emerged in which ChIs are capable of bi-directionally influencing cell-type specific excitability of both medium spiny projection neurons (SPNs) and striatal interneurons (Goldberg et al., 2012; Lim et al., 2014; Oldenburg and Ding, 2011; Higley et al., 2009) and can directly alter the release probability from dopaminergic terminals on relatively rapid timescales (10 s-100s of ms) (Di Chiara et al., 1994; Threlfell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to Goldberg et al., 2012; Lim et al., 2014; Oldenburg and Ding, 2011; Higley et al., 2009.

claim: Cholinergic interneurons can directly alter the release probability from dopaminergic terminals on relatively rapid timescales (10 s-100s of ms).
source: From these studies, a complex picture has emerged in which ChIs are capable of bi-directionally influencing cell-type specific excitability of both medium spiny projection neurons (SPNs) and striatal interneurons (Goldberg et al., 2012; Lim et al., 2014; Oldenburg and Ding, 2011; Higley et al., 2009) and can directly alter the release probability from dopaminergic terminals on relatively rapid timescales (10 s-100s of ms) (Di Chiara et al., 1994; Threlfell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to Di Chiara et al., 1994; Threlfell et al., 2012.

claim: Acetylcholine release can modulate long term pre and post-synaptic plasticity (minutes to days) on medium spiny projection neurons.
source: Ach release can also modulate long term pre and post-synaptic plasticity (minutes to days) on SPNs (Wang et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to Wang et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2016.

claim: Medium spiny projection neurons, interneurons, and dopamine afferents, along with excitatory glutamatergic inputs from thalamus and cortex provide powerful and rapid modulation of the cholinergic interneurons.
source: In turn, SPNs, interneurons, and DA afferents, along with excitatory glutamatergic inputs from thalamus and cortex provide powerful and rapid modulation of the cholinergic interneurons (Aosaki et al., 1994b; Ding et al., 2010; Di Chiara et al., 1994; Matsumoto et al., 2001; Raz et al., 1996; Straub et al., 2014; Witten et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2018; Zucca et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to Aosaki et al., 1994b; Ding et al., 2010; Di Chiara et al., 1994; Matsumoto et al., 2001; Raz et al., 1996; Straub et al., 2014; Witten et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2018; Zucca et al., 2018.

claim: Electrophysiological measurements of naturally occurring cholinergic interneuron signaling in behaving animals have to date been limited to only a few (typically 2–4) putative cholinergic interneurons recorded simultaneously.
source: Electrophysiological measurements of naturally occurring ChI signaling in behaving animals have to date been limited to only a few (typically 2–4) putative ChIs recorded simultaneously and are challenged by difficulties in reliable cell identification.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of prior studies.

claim: Very little change in cholinergic interneuron population signaling was observed when mice were at rest.
source: Very little change in ChI population signaling was observed when mice were at rest but positive going transients were consistently elevated during spontaneous movement (Figure 1B–C; mean DF/F, p<1e-19 Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Positive going transients in cholinergic interneuron population signaling were consistently elevated during spontaneous movement.
source: Very little change in ChI population signaling was observed when mice were at rest but positive going transients were consistently elevated during spontaneous movement (Figure 1B–C; mean DF/F, p<1e-19 Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-C with statistical significance p<1e-19.

claim: Cholinergic interneuron population signals increased rapidly and reliably approximately 100 ms prior to spontaneous movement onsets from rest.
source: ChI population signals increased rapidly and reliably approximately 100 ms prior to spontaneous movement onsets from rest (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: Very small 'micro' movements occurring at velocities and accelerations below rest threshold did not elicit significant cholinergic interneuron responses.
source: Very small 'micro' movements occurring at velocities and accelerations below our rest threshold did not elicit significant ChI responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Movement onsets from rest could be classified into two types: transitions to continuous locomotion and short duration 'jerks'.
source: Broadly, movement onsets from rest could be classified into two types: transitions to continuous locomotion (Figure 1B,G,K) and short duration 'jerks', consisting of rapidly terminated forward and backward movements (Figure 1B,H,L).
evidence: This is a classification based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1.

claim: Significant elevations in cholinergic interneuron signaling were observed for both locomotion initiations and jerks with similar timing and amplitudes.
source: Significant elevations in ChI signaling were observed for both of these movement onset types with similar timing and amplitudes (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G,H.

claim: A gradual decrease in cholinergic interneuron signal to baseline was observed at locomotion terminations.
source: A gradual decrease in ChI signal to baseline was observed at locomotion terminations (Figure 1B,I,M).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,I,M.

claim: During continuous, high velocity locomotion periods, significantly less transient signaling was present in cholinergic interneurons relative to movement onset periods.
source: During continuous, high velocity locomotion periods, significantly less transient signaling was present relative to movement onset periods (Figure 1B,D; p<0.01 Wilcoxon rank-sum test), though transient signaling during these periods was greater than during rest (Figure 1B,D; p<3e-13, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,D with statistical significance p<0.01.

claim: Transient signaling in cholinergic interneurons during continuous locomotion was greater than during rest.
source: During continuous, high velocity locomotion periods, significantly less transient signaling was present relative to movement onset periods (Figure 1B,D; p<0.01 Wilcoxon rank-sum test), though transient signaling during these periods was greater than during rest (Figure 1B,D; p<3e-13, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,D with statistical significance p<3e-13.

claim: The largest cholinergic interneuron transients occurring post-onset were associated with large accelerations at low velocity, corresponding to movement resets in ongoing locomotion.
source: The largest ChI transients (top quartile) occurring post-onset were associated with large accelerations at low velocity, corresponding to movement resets in ongoing locomotion (Figure 1B,J,N, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) where the mouse rapidly transitioned to near rest then re-accelerated to resume locomotion.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,J,N and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Less cholinergic interneuron signal change was associated with accelerations occurring during high velocity, continuous locomotion.
source: Less signal change was associated with accelerations occurring during high velocity, continuous locomotion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Cholinergic interneuron movement related signals were observed in the absence of task contingencies, changes in salient sensory stimuli, and before any exposure to rewards.
source: ChI movement related signals were observed in the absence of task contingencies, changes in salient sensory stimuli, and before any exposure to rewards (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–H.

claim: Transient dorsal striatum cholinergic interneuron population signals reflect rapid transitions in internally generated spontaneous movement, independently of changes in reward prediction or experimentally generated salient stimuli.
source: These results demonstrate that transient dorsal striatum ChI population signals reflect rapid transitions in internally generated spontaneous movement, from rest to movement or during resets in locomotion, independently of changes in reward prediction or experimentally generated salient stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Fiber photometry measures an aggregate weighted average from active cells within a small region (~100–200 µm radius sphere) around the optic fiber.
source: Fiber photometry measures an aggregate weighted average from active cells (cell bodies, axons and dendrites) within a small region (~100–200 µm radius sphere) around the optic fiber (Cui et al., 2013), but single neurons may coordinate in multiple ways to generate the observed population transients (London et al., 2018; Rehani et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the fiber photometry technique, supported by citation to Cui et al., 2013.

claim: Robust transients were observed in both dorsal and ventral cholinergic interneuron recordings from the same mice.
source: Robust transients were observed in both dorsal and ventral recordings from the same mice (Figure 2A), but only dorsal ChI signals rapidly increased at spontaneous movement onsets from rest (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Only dorsal cholinergic interneuron signals rapidly increased at spontaneous movement onsets from rest.
source: Robust transients were observed in both dorsal and ventral recordings from the same mice (Figure 2A), but only dorsal ChI signals rapidly increased at spontaneous movement onsets from rest (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Ventral striatum cholinergic interneuron transients did not exhibit consistent timing with respect to spontaneous mouse accelerations.
source: Moreover, unlike dorsal striatum, ventral striatum transients did not exhibit consistent timing with respect to spontaneous mouse accelerations (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Spontaneous movement signals in cholinergic interneurons are different across the dorsal-ventral axis of the striatum, similar to dopamine projections.
source: These data indicate that, similar to dopamine projections, spontaneous movement signals in ChIs are different across the dorsal-ventral axis of the striatum.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 2, with comparison to cited dopamine studies.

claim: Delivery of unpredicted water rewards elicited responses in dorsal striatum cholinergic interneurons that consisted of a short latency increase followed by a small decrease aligned to the audible solenoid click.
source: Delivery of unpredicted water rewards through a spout near the animals' mouth elicited responses in dorsal striatum ChIs, that on average, consisted of a short latency increase followed by a small decrease aligned to the audible solenoid click associated with water valve opening (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The dorsal striatum cholinergic interneuron response to unpredicted rewards was variable and both the increase and decrease were not reliably present across individual trials.
source: While reminiscent of the previously reported burst/pause observations, this response was variable and both the increase and decrease were not reliably present across individual trials (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Ventral striatum cholinergic interneurons exhibited robust and consistent increases on nearly every trial following reward delivery.
source: In contrast, ventral striatum ChIs exhibited robust and consistent increases on nearly every trial following reward delivery (Figure 2D,I).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D,I.

claim: The dorsal striatum cholinergic interneuron response to unpredicted rewards was significantly positively correlated with changes in velocity at reward delivery.
source: The dorsal striatum ChI response was significantly positively correlated with these changes in velocity at reward delivery (Figure 2F–H, R = 0.48, p<1.7e-8) but the response in ventral striatum was not (Figure 2J–L, R = −0.17, p=0.06).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F–H with statistical significance R = 0.48, p<1.7e-8.

claim: The ventral striatum cholinergic interneuron response to unpredicted rewards was not significantly correlated with changes in velocity at reward delivery.
source: The dorsal striatum ChI response was significantly positively correlated with these changes in velocity at reward delivery (Figure 2F–H, R = 0.48, p<1.7e-8) but the response in ventral striatum was not (Figure 2J–L, R = −0.17, p=0.06).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J–L with statistical result R = −0.17, p=0.06.

claim: Changes in movement at reward consumption could account for much of the dorsal striatum cholinergic interneuron population response to unpredicted rewards.
source: These data indicate that dorsal and ventral ChIs exhibit different responses to unpredicted rewards and that changes in movement at reward consumption could account for much of the dorsal striatum ChI population response.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A prominent triphasic increase/decrease/increase signal was observed in dorsal striatum cholinergic interneurons to a conditioned visual stimulus paired with reward.
source: Notably, we did observe a prominent triphasic increase/decrease/increase signal in dorsal striatum ChIs to a conditioned visual stimulus paired with reward similar to those described in recordings of TANs with electrophysiology (Aosaki et al., 1994a) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,G).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,G.

claim: The dorsal striatum cholinergic interneuron response to conditioned cues could not be fully explained by changes in movement.
source: This response could not be fully explained by changes in movement (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,G), indicating that dorsal striatum ChIs do display a response to conditioned cues that is at least partly independent of movement changes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,G.

claim: Dorsal striatum cholinergic interneurons display a response to conditioned cues that is at least partly independent of movement changes.
source: This response could not be fully explained by changes in movement (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,G), indicating that dorsal striatum ChIs do display a response to conditioned cues that is at least partly independent of movement changes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,G.

claim: Ventral cholinergic interneurons exhibited a sustained increase at the conditioned stimulus onset and a sharp increase at the delivery of the predicted reward.
source: Ventral ChIs, in contrast, exhibited a sustained increase at the CS onset and a sharp increase at the delivery of the predicted reward (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–G) consistent with other rodent ventral TAN recordings (Atallah et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–G.

claim: Ventral cholinergic interneurons exhibited a small increase after movement onsets for sessions after experience with unpredicted rewards but not before.
source: Moreover, ventral ChIs exhibited a small increase after movement onsets for sessions after experience with unpredicted rewards (but not before, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating that ventral ChIs are not sensitive to spontaneous movement per se but may be influenced by changes in reward prediction that coincide with changes in movement, a property also present in ventral striatum dopamine signaling (Ko and Wanat, 2016; Syed et al., 2016) and midbrain cell body firing (Coddington and Dudman, 2018).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Ventral cholinergic interneurons are not sensitive to spontaneous movement per se but may be influenced by changes in reward prediction that coincide with changes in movement.
source: Moreover, ventral ChIs exhibited a small increase after movement onsets for sessions after experience with unpredicted rewards (but not before, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating that ventral ChIs are not sensitive to spontaneous movement per se but may be influenced by changes in reward prediction that coincide with changes in movement, a property also present in ventral striatum dopamine signaling (Ko and Wanat, 2016; Syed et al., 2016) and midbrain cell body firing (Coddington and Dudman, 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, with comparison to cited studies.

claim: Cholinergic interneuron signals differ strikingly in their responses to cues, rewards, and to movement across the dorsal-ventral axis of the striatum, similarly to dorsal-ventral gradients in dopamine signaling.
source: These findings demonstrate that ChI signals differ strikingly in their responses to cues, rewards, and to movement across the dorsal-ventral axis of the striatum, similarly to dorsal-ventral gradients in DA signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Baseline fluorescence in cholinergic interneuron cell bodies presumably reflected ongoing tonic firing.
source: Since ChIs fire tonically at ~3–10 Hz (Wilson et al., 1990), baseline fluorescence in cell bodies presumably reflected ongoing tonic firing, while large Ca2+ transients presumably represented bursts of action potentials (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about ChI firing patterns and GCaMP properties, supported by citations to Wilson et al., 1990 and Chen et al., 2013.

claim: Large calcium transients in cholinergic interneurons presumably represented bursts of action potentials.
source: Since ChIs fire tonically at ~3–10 Hz (Wilson et al., 1990), baseline fluorescence in cell bodies presumably reflected ongoing tonic firing, while large Ca2+ transients presumably represented bursts of action potentials (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about GCaMP properties, supported by citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claim: Nearly all single cholinergic interneurons exhibited significantly larger and more frequent calcium transients during all movement periods relative to rest.
source: Consistent with photometry recordings, nearly all single ChIs exhibited significantly larger and more frequent calcium transients during all movement periods relative to rest (Figure 3E, p=4.1e-87 Wilcoxon rank sum test across all cells, 266/268 cells p<0.01).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E with statistical significance p=4.1e-87.

claim: Single cholinergic interneurons exhibited similar rapid increases to population photometry measures at general movement onsets.
source: Single ChIs exhibited similar rapid increases to population photometry measures at general movement onsets (Figure 3G–H) and increases at jerks and locomotion initiations (Figure 3I–J).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G–H.

claim: Unlike population photometry measures, transient signaling in single cholinergic interneurons was also prominent during continuous locomotion to a similar extent to locomotion onsets.
source: Unlike the population photometry measures, however, transient signaling in single ChIs was also prominent during continuous locomotion to a similar extent to locomotion onsets (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: Imaging the same fields with 800 nm excitation light or in mice expressing td-tomato did not reveal significant positive going transients or rapid increases at movement onsets.
source: Imaging the same fields with 800 nm excitation light (rendering GCaMP fluorescence static, that is non-activity dependent) or in separate mice expressing the static red indicator td-tomato did not reveal significant positive going transients or rapid increases at movement onsets (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating that movement induced artifacts in the fluorescence measurements could not account for the movement-related transients in single ChIs.
evidence: This is a control experiment finding supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Movement induced artifacts in the fluorescence measurements could not account for the movement-related transients in single cholinergic interneurons.
source: Imaging the same fields with 800 nm excitation light (rendering GCaMP fluorescence static, that is non-activity dependent) or in separate mice expressing the static red indicator td-tomato did not reveal significant positive going transients or rapid increases at movement onsets (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating that movement induced artifacts in the fluorescence measurements could not account for the movement-related transients in single ChIs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from control experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Transient encoding of spontaneous movement is present at movement onsets and during continuous locomotion in the majority of dorsal striatum cholinergic interneurons.
source: In summary, transient encoding of spontaneous movement is present at movement onsets and during continuous locomotion in the majority of dorsal striatum ChIs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Transient synchrony across the population of cholinergic interneurons, rather than signaling amplitude across single cells in the population, may be modulated during behavior.
source: The observation that mean transient changes in dorsal striatum ChI population fluorescence as measured with photometry (Figure 1D), but not single cell transients (Figure 3F), decreased from locomotion initiations to continuous locomotion, raised the possibility that transient synchrony across the population of Chls, rather than signaling amplitude across single cells in the population, may be modulated during behavior.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing data in Figure 1D and Figure 3F.

claim: Synchrony of firing across the cholinergic interneuron network has been identified in vitro as an important determinant of its influence on pre-synaptic dopamine release from axon terminals.
source: Synchrony of firing across the ChI network has been identified in vitro as an important determinant of its influence on pre-synaptic dopamine release from axon terminals (Threlfell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation to Threlfell et al., 2012.

claim: High correlations across pairs or triplets of tonically active neurons have been reported to conditioned stimuli and rewards in behaving primates.
source: High correlations across pairs or triplets of TANs have been reported to conditioned stimuli and rewards in behaving primates (Morris et al., 2004; Raz et al., 1996), but synchrony has never been evaluated across larger networks of ChIs (>10) during spontaneous movement.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to Morris et al., 2004; Raz et al., 1996.

claim: Synchrony has never been evaluated across larger networks of cholinergic interneurons (>10) during spontaneous movement.
source: High correlations across pairs or triplets of TANs have been reported to conditioned stimuli and rewards in behaving primates (Morris et al., 2004; Raz et al., 1996), but synchrony has never been evaluated across larger networks of ChIs (>10) during spontaneous movement.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Over all behavior periods, activity across cholinergic interneurons was highly correlated, even for pairs of neurons separated by >400 um.
source: Over all behavior periods, activity across ChIs was highly correlated, even for pairs of neurons separated by >400 um (Figure 4A–E).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A–E.

claim: Transients in cholinergic interneurons were synchronized with a peak at zero phase lag, and this timing was consistent across cell pairs.
source: Transients were synchronized with a peak at zero phase lag, and this timing was consistent across cell pairs (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B–C.

claim: Across all behavior periods, there was a weak but significant negative relationship between the magnitude of pairwise correlations and distance between cholinergic interneuron cell pairs separated by distances < 500 um.
source: Also across all behavior periods, there was a weak but significant negative relationship between the magnitude of pairwise correlations and distance between cell pairs separated by distances < 500 um (R = −0.08, p=0.005, Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D with statistical significance R = −0.08, p=0.005.

claim: Cholinergic interneuron networks are highly synchronized during behavior across large regions of dorsal striatum and positioned to potentially influence dopamine release from local axon terminals.
source: This data indicates that ChI networks are highly synchronized during behavior across large regions of dorsal striatum and positioned to potentially influence dopamine release from local axon terminals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 4, with reference to established mechanisms.

claim: At movement onsets, transients in cholinergic interneurons were highly synchronized.
source: At movement onsets, including both jerks and locomotion initiations, transients were highly synchronized (Figure 4F,H,J; Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and correlations across cell pairs were significantly larger than during rest (p<1e-90, Wilcoxon rank-sum test; Figure 4H–I; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F,H,J.

claim: Correlations across cholinergic interneuron cell pairs at movement onsets were significantly larger than during rest.
source: At movement onsets, including both jerks and locomotion initiations, transients were highly synchronized (Figure 4F,H,J; Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and correlations across cell pairs were significantly larger than during rest (p<1e-90, Wilcoxon rank-sum test; Figure 4H–I; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H–I with statistical significance p<1e-90.

claim: At movement onsets, there was a significant negative correlation between cell-cell correlation and anatomical distance in cholinergic interneurons, not present during rest periods.
source: Moreover, there was a significant negative correlation at onsets between cell-cell correlation and anatomical distance, not present during rest periods (p<1e-9, R = −0.26, Figure 4H,J,L; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H,J,L with statistical significance p<1e-9, R = −0.26.

claim: Correlations between cholinergic interneuron cell pairs and number of activated neurons per transient were significantly lower during continuous running periods on average than at onsets or at rest.
source: Importantly, correlations between cell pairs and number of activated neurons per transient were significantly lower during continuous running periods on average than at onsets or at rest (Figure 4G–L; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), but like onsets, there was a strong negative relationship between cell pair correlation and distance (r = −0.42, p<1e-9; Figure 4K).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G–L.

claim: During continuous locomotion, there was a strong negative relationship between cholinergic interneuron cell pair correlation and distance.
source: Importantly, correlations between cell pairs and number of activated neurons per transient were significantly lower during continuous running periods on average than at onsets or at rest (Figure 4G–L; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), but like onsets, there was a strong negative relationship between cell pair correlation and distance (r = −0.42, p<1e-9; Figure 4K).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4K with statistical significance r = −0.42, p<1e-9.

claim: Synchrony was lower during continuous locomotion despite larger overall mean ΔF/F relative to onsets or rest.
source: Synchrony was lower during continuous locomotion despite larger overall mean DF/F relative to onsets or rest (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 4.

claim: Synchrony and functional spatial organization across cholinergic interneurons is not fixed, but changes with an animal's movement state.
source: These results indicate that synchrony and functional spatial organization across ChIs is not fixed, but changes with an animal's movement state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The decrease in cholinergic interneuron population transient signaling measured with photometry during continuous running relative to locomotion onset is not likely a result of decreased transient amplitudes in single cholinergic interneurons, but reflects decreased synchrony of transients.
source: The decrease in ChI population transient signaling measured with photometry during continuous running (Figure 1D,E,G) relative to locomotion onset is therefore not likely a result of decreased transient amplitudes in single ChIs (Figure 3F), but reflects decreased synchrony of transients (Figure 4F–K).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing data in Figures 1, 3, and 4.

claim: Sub-second timescale signals in striatum cholinergic interneuron networks vary with respect to changes in spontaneous movement states.
source: The data presented thus far provides evidence that sub-second timescale signals in striatum Chl networks vary with respect to changes in spontaneous movement states.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figures 1-4.

claim: Substantia nigra pars compacta cell bodies, dopamine projection axons in dorsal striatum, and dopamine release rapidly fluctuate to spontaneous locomotor accelerations and decelerations.
source: Previous work has shown that SNc cell bodies, dopamine projection axons in dorsal striatum, and dopamine release rapidly fluctuate to spontaneous locomotor accelerations and decelerations and likely influence movement drive on sub-second timescales via rapid modulation of striatum output pathways (Howe and Dombeck, 2016; da Silva et al., 2018; Patriarchi et al., 2018; Coddington and Dudman, 2018; Dodson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to Howe and Dombeck, 2016; da Silva et al., 2018; Patriarchi et al., 2018; Coddington and Dudman, 2018; Dodson et al., 2016.

claim: Dopamine signaling likely influences movement drive on sub-second timescales via rapid modulation of striatum output pathways.
source: Previous work has shown that SNc cell bodies, dopamine projection axons in dorsal striatum, and dopamine release rapidly fluctuate to spontaneous locomotor accelerations and decelerations and likely influence movement drive on sub-second timescales via rapid modulation of striatum output pathways (Howe and Dombeck, 2016; da Silva et al., 2018; Patriarchi et al., 2018; Coddington and Dudman, 2018; Dodson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to Howe and Dombeck, 2016; da Silva et al., 2018; Patriarchi et al., 2018; Coddington and Dudman, 2018; Dodson et al., 2016.

claim: Signaling in dorsal striatum dopamine axons was highly synchronized across the two hemispheres with zero phase lag.
source: We first established that signaling in dorsal striatum dopamine axons was highly synchronized across the two-hemispheres with zero phase lag (DAT-cre, n = 4; Figure 5A,D,E; mean phase lag DA v DA 0.6 ms, S.E.M 3.5 ms).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,D,E.

claim: Cholinergic interneuron population signals were highly synchronized across the two hemispheres of the dorsal striatum with zero phase lag.
source: We then determined that ChI population signals were similarly highly synchronized across the two-hemispheres of the dorsal striatum with zero phase lag (ChAT-cre, n = 6; Figure 5B,F,G; mean phase lag ChI vs ChI 0 ms, S.E.M 5.4 ms).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B,F,G.

claim: Dopamine and cholinergic interneuron population transients during locomotion likely reflect general changes in movement state, rather than the kinematics of specific limbs.
source: These new findings indicate that DA and ChI population transients during locomotion likely reflect general changes in movement state, rather than the kinematics of specific limbs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data showing bilateral synchrony in Figure 5.

claim: Peak cross-correlations between signals from dorsal striatum cholinergic interneurons and contralateral dopamine axons was significantly lower than for dopamine/dopamine or cholinergic interneuron/cholinergic interneuron bilateral comparisons.
source: Notably, peak cross-correlations between signals from dorsal striatum ChIs and contralateral DA axons was significantly lower than for DA/DA or ChI/ChI bilateral comparisons regardless of which hemispheres the ChI/DA axon signals were recorded (p<1e-10, Wilcoxon rank-sum test; Figure 5J, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J with statistical significance p<1e-10.

claim: The peak and trough in the dopamine/cholinergic interneuron cross correlations were significantly phase offset from 0 in all recordings.
source: In addition, the peak and trough in the DA/ChI cross correlations were significantly phase offset from 0 in all recordings (Figure 5C,H,I,K; mean peak lag +114 ms, mean trough lag −180 ms), regardless of hemisphere (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C,H,I,K.

claim: The peak in correlation at positive lag indicates an increase in dopamine lagging an increase in cholinergic interneuron signal.
source: The peak in correlation at positive lag indicates an increase in dopamine lagging an increase in ChI signal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cross-correlation data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The timing offsets between cholinergic interneurons and dopamine axon signals could not be attributed to different calcium dynamics between the subcellular compartments recorded.
source: These timing offsets between ChIs and DA axon signals could not be attributed to different calcium dynamics between the subcellular compartments recorded (Figure 5M, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from control experiments shown in Figure 5M and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: Simultaneous recordings from dopaminergic substantia nigra pars compacta cell bodies and dopamine axons from the same hemisphere were correlated at near zero phase lag.
source: Simultaneous recordings from dopaminergic SNc cell bodies and DA axons from the same hemisphere were correlated at near zero phase lag (Figure 5L,M) indicating that the DA/ChI timing differences are unlikely to be accounted for by axon transmission delays, which are estimated to be less ~15 ms for DA axons (Pissadaki and Bolam, 2013).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5L,M.

claim: The dopamine/cholinergic interneuron timing differences are unlikely to be accounted for by axon transmission delays.
source: Simultaneous recordings from dopaminergic SNc cell bodies and DA axons from the same hemisphere were correlated at near zero phase lag (Figure 5L,M) indicating that the DA/ChI timing differences are unlikely to be accounted for by axon transmission delays, which are estimated to be less ~15 ms for DA axons (Pissadaki and Bolam, 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 5L,M, with reference to cited estimates.

claim: Very little signal and low correlations were detected from the striatum contralateral to the substantia nigra pars compacta injected hemisphere in DAT-cre mice injected unilaterally.
source: Finally, very little signal and low correlations were detected from the striatum contralateral to the SNc injected hemisphere in DAT-cre mice injected unilaterally (Figure 5N–O; No Chl labeling), indicating little contribution from contralateral SNc projections or from other sources such as intrinsic fluorescence.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5N–O.

claim: There is little contribution from contralateral substantia nigra pars compacta projections or from other sources such as intrinsic fluorescence to the dopamine axon signals measured.
source: Finally, very little signal and low correlations were detected from the striatum contralateral to the SNc injected hemisphere in DAT-cre mice injected unilaterally (Figure 5N–O; No Chl labeling), indicating little contribution from contralateral SNc projections or from other sources such as intrinsic fluorescence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 5N–O.

claim: Dopamine axon terminals and cholinergic interneurons exhibit different relative timing and amplitude variations relative to spontaneous movement.
source: These results establish a new approach for simultaneously monitoring DA and ChI signaling in striatum on sub-second timescales during behavior and indicate that DA axon terminals and ChIs exhibit different relative timing and amplitude variations relative to spontaneous movement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Dopamine axon transient signaling, like cholinergic interneurons, was stronger during movement periods relative to rest.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Howe and Dombeck, 2016; Patriarchi et al., 2018), DA axon transient signaling, like ChIs, was stronger during movement periods relative to rest (p<1e-6 Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,B with statistical significance p<1e-6.

claim: Considered across all movement periods, both cholinergic interneurons and dopamine axons were significantly correlated to acceleration and velocity but with different relative timing.
source: Also, considered across all movement periods, both ChIs and DA axons were significantly correlated to acceleration and velocity but with different relative timing (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Movement onsets from rest, on average, were associated with an increase in mean dopamine signaling relative to rest.
source: Movement onsets from rest (all jerks, initiations, and unclassified), on average, were associated with an increase in mean DA signaling relative to rest (Figure 6E; p<0.01 Wilcoxon rank-sum).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E with statistical significance p<0.01.

claim: The increase in dopamine signaling at movement onsets was smaller relative to that in cholinergic interneurons because of both a higher dopamine signal at rest and a smaller average increase at onsets.
source: This increase was smaller relative to that in ChIs (Figure 6F) because of both a higher DA signal at rest and a smaller average increase at onsets (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: Unlike cholinergic interneurons, dopamine axons exhibited elevated mean signaling during continuous locomotion relative to onsets.
source: Unlike ChIs, however, DA axons exhibited elevated mean signaling during continuous locomotion relative to onsets (Figure 6E, p<0.01 Wilcoxon rank-sum).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E with statistical significance p<0.01.

claim: Dopamine and cholinergic interneurons both respond to spontaneous changes in movement, but their contribution to distinct movement states may not be equivalent.
source: These data indicate that DA and ChIs both respond to spontaneous changes in movement, but their contribution to distinct movement states may not be equivalent.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Both dopamine and cholinergic interneurons increased rapidly at the initiations of long locomotion bouts, with dopamine signaling slightly lagging cholinergic interneurons.
source: Both increased rapidly at the initiations of long locomotion bouts, with DA signaling slightly lagging ChIs (Figure 6G,I, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G,I.

claim: At the onsets of rapidly terminated jerks, dopamine axon population signals rapidly decreased below rest baseline, while cholinergic interneuron populations increased to a level similar to locomotion bout initiations.
source: However, at the onsets of rapidly terminated jerks (initiation and termination within ~1 s), DA axon population signals rapidly decreased below rest baseline, while ChI populations increased to a level similar to locomotion bout initiations (Figure 6G–J, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G–J.

claim: Population cholinergic interneuron transients occurring at rest were strongly predictive of subsequent transitions to movement.
source: Consistent with this finding, population ChI transients occurring at rest, while strongly predictive of subsequent transitions to movement (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), were associated with significantly larger increases in velocity when they were accompanied by large DA axon signal increases (Figure 6K,M, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cholinergic interneuron transients at rest were associated with significantly larger increases in velocity when they were accompanied by large dopamine axon signal increases.
source: Consistent with this finding, population ChI transients occurring at rest, while strongly predictive of subsequent transitions to movement (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), were associated with significantly larger increases in velocity when they were accompanied by large DA axon signal increases (Figure 6K,M, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6K,M.

claim: Dopamine axon signaling at rest alone was only weakly predictive of transitions to movement.
source: Interestingly, DA axon signaling at rest alone was only weakly predictive of transitions to movement (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), and DA transients in the absence of accompanying ChI signal were not associated with significant increases in velocity above rest (Figure 6L–M, Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Dopamine transients in the absence of accompanying cholinergic interneuron signal were not associated with significant increases in velocity above rest.
source: Interestingly, DA axon signaling at rest alone was only weakly predictive of transitions to movement (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), and DA transients in the absence of accompanying ChI signal were not associated with significant increases in velocity above rest (Figure 6L–M, Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6L–M.

claim: Dopamine and cholinergic interneuron signals can either converge or diverge with changes in movement from rest and may play complementary roles in controlling onsets.
source: These results indicate that DA and ChI signals can either converge or diverge with changes in movement from rest and may play complementary roles in controlling onsets.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Synchronized cholinergic interneuron network transients signal a transition in the movement state (rest to move).
source: Synchronized ChI network transients signal a transition in the movement state (rest to move) while the subsequent DA signals indicate whether that movement is facilitated (DA increase, locomotion initiation) or rapidly terminated (DA decrease, jerk).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Subsequent dopamine signals indicate whether movement is facilitated (dopamine increase, locomotion initiation) or rapidly terminated (dopamine decrease, jerk).
source: Synchronized ChI network transients signal a transition in the movement state (rest to move) while the subsequent DA signals indicate whether that movement is facilitated (DA increase, locomotion initiation) or rapidly terminated (DA decrease, jerk).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Dopamine and cholinergic interneuron signals correlated positively with each other at locomotion initiations and negatively at jerks.
source: While DA and ChI signals correlated positively with each other at locomotion initiations and negatively at jerks (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), continuous locomotion periods were associated with a strong negative correlation on average between DA axon and ChI population signals, indicating a ChI population decrease following a DA population increase (Figure 7A–C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Continuous locomotion periods were associated with a strong negative correlation on average between dopamine axon and cholinergic interneuron population signals.
source: While DA and ChI signals correlated positively with each other at locomotion initiations and negatively at jerks (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), continuous locomotion periods were associated with a strong negative correlation on average between DA axon and ChI population signals, indicating a ChI population decrease following a DA population increase (Figure 7A–C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A–C.

claim: Both dopamine and cholinergic interneuron signals were correlated similarly to rapid changes in acceleration during locomotion.
source: Both signals were correlated similarly to rapid changes in acceleration during locomotion (Figure 7D, indicating a slight lag between rapid acceleration and increases in ChI or DA signal).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Dopamine signaling showed a positive peak correlation with velocity at near zero phase lag during continuous locomotion.
source: However, DA and ChI populations were correlated very differently with velocity: DA signaling showed a positive peak correlation with velocity at near zero phase lag, while ChI signals showed a negative trough in the correlation at positive lags (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Cholinergic interneuron signals showed a negative trough in the correlation with velocity at positive lags during continuous locomotion.
source: However, DA and ChI populations were correlated very differently with velocity: DA signaling showed a positive peak correlation with velocity at near zero phase lag, while ChI signals showed a negative trough in the correlation at positive lags (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Velocity increases during continuous locomotion were associated with a coordinated increase in dopamine signal followed by a decrease in cholinergic interneuron population synchrony.
source: These findings indicate that velocity increases during continuous locomotion were associated with a coordinated increase in DA signal followed by a decrease in ChI population synchrony (Figures 4 and 7F–G).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 7F–G.

claim: Decreases in velocity during continuous locomotion were associated with decreases in dopamine signal, followed by increases in cholinergic interneuron synchrony.
source: Conversely, decreases in velocity were associated with decreases in DA signal, followed by increases in ChI synchrony (Figure 7F,H).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F,H.

claim: When synchronous cholinergic interneuron population transients occurred during continuous locomotion, they were associated with rapid decreases in velocity when not accompanied by strong dopamine signals.
source: When synchronous ChI population transients occurred during continuous locomotion, they were associated with rapid decreases in velocity when not accompanied by strong DA signals, but were associated with increases in velocity or 'resets' in locomotion when DA and ChI population signals occurred in conjunction (Figure 7A,I–J, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A,I–J.

claim: Synchronous cholinergic interneuron population transients during continuous locomotion were associated with increases in velocity or 'resets' in locomotion when dopamine and cholinergic interneuron population signals occurred in conjunction.
source: When synchronous ChI population transients occurred during continuous locomotion, they were associated with rapid decreases in velocity when not accompanied by strong DA signals, but were associated with increases in velocity or 'resets' in locomotion when DA and ChI population signals occurred in conjunction (Figure 7A,I–J, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A,I–J.

claim: At locomotion terminations to rest, relative cholinergic interneuron population signaling increased slightly prior to movement cessation, while dopamine signals decreased with the drop in velocity.
source: At locomotion terminations to rest, relative ChI population signaling increased slightly prior to movement cessation, while DA signals decreased with the drop in velocity (Figure 7K).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7K.

claim: Fluctuations in running speed during continuous locomotion are associated with divergent patterns of dorsal striatum cholinergic interneuron and dopamine network activity.
source: These data indicate that fluctuations in running speed during continuous locomotion are associated with divergent patterns of dorsal striatum ChI and DA network activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Increases in the speed or vigor of ongoing locomotion were associated with increases in dopamine population signals followed by drops in cholinergic interneuron population synchrony associated with movement state transitions.
source: Increases in the speed or vigor of ongoing locomotion were associated with increases in DA population signals followed by drops in ChI population synchrony associated with movement state transitions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Velocity decreases during continuous locomotion were marked by coincident decreases in dopamine population signal, followed by increases in cholinergic interneuron synchrony as movement state transitions became more likely.
source: Velocity decreases, in contrast, were marked by coincident decreases in DA population signal, followed by increases in ChI synchrony as movement state transitions became more likely (locomotion resets and terminations).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Cholinergic interneuron population transients may mark movement state transitions, which are either enacted and invigorated (dopamine increase) or terminated (dopamine decrease).
source: Thus, ChI population transients may mark movement state transitions, which are either enacted and invigorated (DA increase) or terminated (DA decrease).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental data shown in Figures 6-7.

claim: Synchronous cholinergic interneuron network activations support rapid changes or reconfigurations in the striatum network that can facilitate general, internally triggered changes in movement state.
source: We hypothesize that synchronous ChI network activations support rapid changes or reconfigurations in the striatum network that can facilitate general, internally triggered changes in movement state (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on experimental findings.

claim: Dopamine and acetylcholine may act both synergistically and competitively to regulate different aspects of movement.
source: This coordination varies dynamically as a function of the animals' behavioral state, suggesting that dopamine and acetylcholine may act both synergistically and competitively to regulate different aspects of movement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figures 5-7.

claim: GCaMP6f expression was confirmed in ChAT+ cells of the ventral striatum (NAc core) of ChAT-cre mice.
source: GCaMP6f expression was confirmed in ChAT+ cells of the ventral striatum (NAc core) of ChAT-cre mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is a methodological finding supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: 97.3% (SD 2.3%) of GCaMP6f expressing neurons in dorsal striatum showed confirmed co-expression of ChAT.
source: Summary of the percent of GCaMP6f expressing neurons with confirmed co-expression of ChAT from three mice (n = 100, 69, and 50 cells in each respective mouse in dorsal striatum and n = 68, 33, and 46 neurons in ventral striatum).
evidence: This is a quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: 98.3% (SD 1.5%) of GCaMP6f expressing neurons in ventral striatum showed confirmed co-expression of ChAT.
source: Summary of the percent of GCaMP6f expressing neurons with confirmed co-expression of ChAT from three mice (n = 100, 69, and 50 cells in each respective mouse in dorsal striatum and n = 68, 33, and 46 neurons in ventral striatum).
evidence: This is a quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.
